chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Black-Scholes Formula, Step by Step

lessons.title: Breaking Down d1, d2, and What N(d1) and N(d2) Actually Mean

children.text: Every idea from the last five lessons, replication, risk-neutral probability, lognormal prices, compresses into one line for a call option.

body.caption: S₀ is today's price, K the strike, r the risk-free rate, T time to expiry in years. N() is a specific function you are about to unpack completely, and d1, d2 are two numbers built from the same five inputs.

children.text: Read it as two present values sitting side by side. The second term, K e^(−rT) N(d2), is what you owe: the strike price, discounted back to today, weighted by the chance you will actually end up paying it. The first term, S0 N(d1), is what you get in return, similarly weighted. A call's value is the weighted, discounted value of what you receive minus what you pay.
What N() Means: The Cumulative Normal Distribution

N(x) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution: the probability that a standard normal random variable lands at or below x. It always outputs a number between 0 and 1, and by the symmetry of the bell curve, N(0) = 0.5 exactly.

body.caption: A few reference values of N(x)

cells: About a 2.3% chance of landing this far below the mean or lower
About a 15.9% chance of landing this far below the mean or lower
Exactly a coin flip: half the distribution lies below zero

children.text: d1 and d2: Standardizing the Distance to the Strike

body.caption: d1 and d2 differ by exactly one term, σ√T, the same scale-of-uncertainty term from Lesson 2.3's volatility annualization.

children.text: Each piece has a name you already know. ln(S0/K) measures how far, in percentage terms, the spot price sits from the strike, positive when in the money, negative when out of it. (r ± σ²/2)T is the risk-neutral drift accumulated over the option's life, the exact term from Lesson 2.2's lognormal price formula once you swap in the risk-free rate for μ, as Lesson 3.1 said you are allowed to do. σ√T is how much uncertainty has built up by expiry: a bigger σ or a longer T stretches this term, which shrinks d1 and d2 toward zero and pulls both N() values toward 50%, exactly the "maximum uncertainty" idea from Lesson 1.2's ATM discussion. In short, d2 is nothing more than the option's log-distance to the strike, measured in standard deviations of uncertainty.

body.title: Optional: proving N(d2) is really a probability

children.text: Lesson 3.1 established that a derivative can be priced using risk-neutral probabilities, which means the risk-neutral version of Lesson 2.2's lognormal formula simply swaps the real-world drift μ for the risk-free rate r. A call finishes in the money exactly when ST exceeds K, so solve that inequality directly for the standard normal variable Z.

content.latex: \begin{aligned} S_T &> K \\ S_0\, e^{(r-\sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt{T}\,Z} &> K \\ Z &> -\frac{\ln(S_0/K) + (r-\sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} = -d_2 \\ P(S_T > K) &= P(Z > -d_2) = N(d_2) \end{aligned}
content.caption: The last step uses the standard normal distribution's symmetry: the probability of being above −d2 equals the probability of being below d2. That is N(d2), by definition, and it is exactly the risk-neutral probability that the call finishes in the money.

children.text: That is why the strike-payment term in the formula is weighted by N(d2): it is, precisely, the risk-neutral probability that you will actually end up paying the strike at all.

N(d1) is the harder one to picture cleanly, because it is not simply "the probability of finishing in the money", that is N(d2)'s job. N(d1) is the weight the formula puts on receiving the stock itself, and it turns out to equal the option's delta, the exact same hedge ratio Lesson 1.3 solved by hand for a single step. Chapter 4 proves this properly and puts it to work; for now, take it as the formula quietly reusing a concept you already built with your own arithmetic three lessons ago.

body.title: Read the formula's anatomy
body.question: In C = S0 N(d1) − K e^(−rT) N(d2), which piece represents the present value of the strike price you might have to pay, weighted by the risk-neutral chance you actually pay it?
body.explanation: K e^(−rT) discounts the strike to today's rupees, and N(d2) is exactly the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money, so this term is the present value of what you might owe, weighted by how likely you are to owe it.

body.title: Use the symmetry of N()
body.prompt: For some option, the numbers work out so that d2 lands at exactly 0. What is N(d2) in that case?
body.explanation: N(0) = 0.5 always, since the standard normal distribution is symmetric around zero. When d2 = 0, this option's risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money is exactly 50%, the same "maximum uncertainty" condition you first saw at the ATM strike in Lesson 1.2.

children.text: The Put Formula, by the Same Logic

body.caption: Same d1 and d2 as the call, just flipped in sign. N(−d2) is the risk-neutral probability that the put finishes in the money, meaning ST ends up below K.

children.text: You do not need to re-derive this from scratch. Lesson 3.4 shows a direct, purely algebraic relationship, put-call parity, that connects the call and put formulas to each other without repeating the probability argument. For now, notice that the two formulas share every input and every d1, d2 calculation; only which side is being weighted by which probability flips.

body.text: d1 and d2 are not arbitrary algebra. They are the option's log-distance to the strike, measured in standard deviations of accumulated uncertainty, and N() converts that distance directly into a risk-neutral probability.

points: The Black-Scholes call formula, C = S0 N(d1) − K e^(−rT) N(d2), is two present values: what you receive, minus what you pay, each weighted by a probability.
N(x) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, always between 0 and 1, with N(0) = 0.5 by symmetry.

d2 = [ln(S0/K) + (r − σ²/2)T] / (σ√T) is the option's log-distance to the strike measured in standard deviations, and N(d2) is exactly the risk-neutral probability the call finishes in the money, provable directly from Lesson 2.2's lognormal formula under Lesson 3.1's risk-neutral drift.
N(d1) weights the stock-received term and turns out to equal the option's delta, previewing Chapter 4.
The put formula, P = K e^(−rT) N(−d2) − S0 N(−d1), reuses the same d1 and d2; Lesson 3.4 connects the two formulas directly via put-call parity.
